title: Fusion-aware latency smoothing and KV prewarm notes
content:
Context and motivation:

We keep seeing two recurring operational failure modes when deploying fused-attention kernels with paged KV in production: (1) 95th/99th latency spikes during brief bursts of long-context requests, and (2) oscillation between heavily fused kernels (good throughput) and unfused fallbacks (higher tail) when KV page misses cascade. This doc captures an initial set of heuristics and lightweight kernel-side mechanisms intended to smooth latency while preserving most of the cost/throughput benefits of fusion/FlashAttention-style kernels, plus a KV prewarm strategy to reduce page miss warmups on sudden context growth.

High-level idea:

- Fusion-aware latency smoothing: add a thin runtime shim that adjusts kernel-launch packing and inference of fusion eligibility on a per-request and short-window basis. Avoid abrupt shifts from fused -> unfused by introducing "soft-fusion" launches that deliberately bound worst-case launch durations and speculative-prefetch if certain heuristics indicate imminent KV usage.

- KV prewarm windowing: when a request is detected to be growing context (e.g., chat history + long user message) or when sequence-length distribution for a customer shifts upward, proactively prewarm recent KV pages on the active device before the fused kernel executes. Prewarm is implemented as an async low-priority kernel that touches page headers + first cache-line to cause page residency without reading full large pages.

Design primitives and rationale:

1) Fusion-eligibility scoring
- Every model shard maintains a short exponential moving average (EMA) of three metrics: seq_len, observed_kv_pages, and avg_inflight_tokens.
- Compute fusion_score = w1 * norm(seq_len) + w2 * norm(observed_kv_pages) - w3 * norm(avg_inflight_tokens_tail). Tunable weights but default w1=0.5, w2=0.4, w3=0.3. Norms map to [0,1] by precomputed model-profile distributions.
- If fusion_score > 0.6 -> attempt full fusion path; if between 0.3-0.6 -> soft-fusion; < 0.3 -> non-fused conservative path.

Why: pure binary decisions cause mode-flip thrash. Soft-fusion provides intermediate code path using lighter-weight fusion (fewer stages fused) with tighter latency bounds.

2) Soft-fusion kernel characteristics
- Fuse compute kernels only where latency-critical (attention & softmax) but keep KV manager calls separated (no page-evictions inside the fused kernel). Implement limited inline prefetch for next-KV-window but avoid heavy blocking operations.
- Upper bound worst-case duration by yielding control in-kernel at pre-defined token boundaries (micro-yield points) — essentially cooperative preemption checkpoints for prefetched streams.

3) Speculative KV prefetch tiers
- Tier 0 (cheap touch): 32B touch of page header + first cache line. Non-blocking, low priority stream. Low GPU time, high hit probability for tiny pages.
- Tier 1 (partial load): copy first N rows of KV tile (configurable, default N=8) to prefetch buffer. Used when tier0 hit-ratio is low but still desire to reduce miss cost.
- Tier 2 (full load): complete page load, used during scheduled warmups (e.g., reserved bursts / canary runs).

4) Prewarm triggers
- Heuristic triggers: sudden increase in seq_len EMA (>2x baseline in last 1s window), explicit route annotation (customer indicates long-history incoming), or model rollout flags (new model variant likely to increase KV usage).
- Cooling: track prewarm_count per node and exponential backoff if prewarm produces little subsequent KV usage. Avoid over-eager prewarm in noisy environments.

5) In-kernel backoff and fallback
- Kernel detects excessive page faults or busy-page stalls and marks a sticky low-fusion suitability flag for the request's routing key for the next T seconds (default T=2s). This prevents repeated expensive fallback oscillations when page-pressure is transient.

Micro-batching + launch smoothing

- Adaptive micro-batching window: If the fusion_score indicates high fusion suitability but current tail latency increases, decrease batch waiting window, favoring immediate launch with soft-fusion path to reduce queuing-induced tail. Conversely, if throughput halved and tail OK, widen window.

- Launch smoothing: rather than immediately switching kernel binary, maintain a short rolling tranche of launched kernels across the three code paths (full fusion, soft-fusion, conservative) according to fusion_score probabilities (e.g., 70/20/10). Helps smooth GPU kernel queue behavior and latency variance.

Runtime state and data structures (sketch)

- small per-shard struct (approx 256B) kept in host pinned memory with: last_seq_len_ema, last_kv_pages_ema, inflight_tail_ema, fusion_score, last_prewarm_ts, sticky_low_fusion_until. Exposed to scheduler and profile traces.

- Prefetch queue: lock-free ring per GPU for tier-0 touches. Tier-1/2 use a prioritized async worker queue (bounded). Prefetch actions are tagged with request-id and route for telemetry.

Telemetry and metrics to collect

- prewarm_trigger_rate, prewarm_success_rate (how often subsequent operations touched prewarmed pages), prewarm_cost_ms (GPU time), fusion_path_ratio (full/soft/none), per-route tail latency delta after prewarm, kernel_oscillation_count (switches between full-fusion and conservative per minute).

Initial microbench experiments (summary)

- Setup: 8x A100s, GPT-2 style transformer, paged-KV tile size 256 rows. Baseline: full fusion w/o prewarm. Workload: 95% short (seq=64), 5% burst long (seq=2048) with poisson bursts.

- Baseline results: avg latency short=12ms, avg latency long=380ms, p99 long spikes often >700ms during first long after cold pages.

- With soft-fusion + tier0 prewarm (touch only): avg short=13.5ms (+12%), avg long=390ms (+2.6%), p99 long reduced median from 720ms->420ms on first-long after cold. Prewarm GPU time negligible (~0.03ms per prewarm touch) but host scheduling overhead measurable.

- With tier1 partial loads (N=8 rows): avg long = 335ms (-12%), p99 long ~360ms. Prewarm GPU time ~0.25ms per prewarm; increased bandwidth but still <2% added device utilization under our test burst rates.

Operational considerations and failure modes

- Over-eager prewarm when traffic pattern noisy -> wasted GPU bandwidth. Mitigation: per-route backoff + require 2x seq_len EMA sustained for prewarm unless explicit override from product.
- Prefetch storms across many concurrent routes -> can saturate PCIe/NVLink. Mitigation: global prefetch rate limiter and prioritization by customer tier.

Open implementation checkpoints (TODOs)

- [ ] Implement tier-0 touch as low-priority CUDA stream and measure host->device scheduling overhead in our runtime (Hannah)
- [ ] Wire fusion_score into scheduler decision path and expose tunable weights via model profile (Diego)
- [ ] Add sticky-low-fusion flag persistence to avoid oscillation across short bursts (Arjun)
- [ ] Build dashboards for prewarm_success_rate and kernel_oscillation_count (Priya)
- [ ] Run larger scale canary across dedicated cluster with mixed customers to validate global prefetch limiter thresholds (infra)

Notes to self / random brainstorms:

- Could we repurpose small on-GPU bloom filter or compact LRU hint to predict hot KV pages based on recent token n-grams? Might help avoid prewarm for high-entropy prompts.
- Consider giving customer-annotated hints via API (e.g., allow route header X-anticipated-context-len: 2048) so clients that know will reduce noise and avoid heuristics.
- Evaluate compression of tier-1 partial rows to reduce prewarm bandwidth.

Links / references:

- internal GH experiments: GH-rt/issue/4823 (prefetch prototypes)
- related design: JIRA-RT-927 (paged-KV architecture notes)

Small appendix: example pseudocode for prewarm decision (host side)

if (fusion_score > 0.4 && seq_len_ema > baseline_seq_len * 1.8) {
  if (now - last_prewarm_ts > prewarm_backoff(route)) {
    enqueue_prefetch(route, request_id, tier=0);
    last_prewarm_ts = now;
  }
}

End.
